nodes.description: TBR1 holds early-born layer 6 neurons in a corticothalamic identity by repressing Fezf2 and CTIP2. Without it, layer 6 markers are reduced, layer 5 subcerebral markers expand, and early-born neurons send axons to subcerebral targets. Neonatal TBR1 dosage in layer 6 is also required for dendritic patterning and synaptogenesis.

evidence.reference_title: Tbr1 and Fezf2 regulate alternate corticofugal neuronal identities during neocortical development.
evidence.snippet: In Tbr1(-/-) mice, the number of cells expressing layer 6 markers was reduced, and the number of cells expressing layer 5 markers was increased.

nodes.description: Tbr1 heterozygous amygdalae fail to induce GRIN2B and activate neurons on behavioral stimulation, and thalamic-lateral amygdala synapses show AMPA and NMDA receptor hypofunction. Raising amygdalar activity with the partial NMDA receptor agonist D-cycloserine, or dietary zinc, rescues behavior in mice.

nodes.description: In Tbr1-deficient mice, early-born preplate and layer 6 neurons are abnormal: Cajal-Retzius cells make less Reelin, producing a reeler-like neuronal migration disorder, subplate differentiation is impaired, and thalamocortical, corticothalamic and callosal projections are misrouted. This is the proposed basis for the cortical malformations seen in some patients, although that link has not been tested directly.

nodes.description: TBR1 homodimerizes and binds co-regulators including FOXP2, FOXP1, BCL11A and CASK, all products of other neurodevelopmental disorder genes. Pathogenic TBR1 variants disrupt these interactions, which may connect TBR1 haploinsufficiency to the language deficits shared with FOXP1- and FOXP2-related disorders.

nodes.description: TBR1 binds near and regulates many genes implicated in autism, including Auts2, Wnt7b, the NMDA receptor subunit gene GRIN2B (with its partner CASK) and axon-guidance and adhesion genes such as Ntng1, Cntn2 and Cdh8. Reduced TBR1 dosage misexpresses these targets in deep cortical layers and amygdala.

The disease mechanism is loss of function.
